items.t: A year to forget for Naspers and Prosus
sum: Prosus and Naspers CEO Fabricio Bloisi’s herculean target of growing the group’s market capitalisation to $168bn (about R2.8-trillion) by 2028 suffered a major blow following 30%-plus plunges this year in the share prices of both companies, which shed more than R800bn in value.

Two years ago the group’s board dangled a $100m “moonshot” award for Bloisi should he meet the lofty target, a bigger number than the present market caps of such giants as SoftBank, PayPal, Shopify and Airbnb.

Despite the plunge in the share price, Naspers and Prosus still carry weighty market valuations on the JSE. Naspers is valued at R540bn, down 33% year to date, while Prosus has shed 34% of its value this year, dragging its market capitalisation to R1.44-trillion.
Naspers, for the first time in more than a decade, now lags Capitec, whose market value has shot up to R570bn after a 17% rally this year.

Allan Gray portfolio manager Rory Kutisker-Jacobson said Napers and Prosus were two of the worst-performing shares year to date. “They are effectively the same company, with Chinese technology group Tencent as their primary asset,” Kutisker-Jacobson said.

“Despite reporting strong full-year earnings, the share prices of Naspers and Prosus are both down over 30%, as investors have become sceptical of Tencent’s AI spending and the long-term risks AI poses to its business model,” he said.
Tencent’s share price has wilted in 2026, sliding roughly 35% amid a broader selloff driven by aggressive AI capital expenditures and looming US semiconductor restrictions.

items.t: Prosus stock buyback covers 2.78 million shares
sum: Prosus repurchased 2.78 million of its own shares between November 2 and November 6, according to an announcement published by Prosus on Tuesday, November 10. The transaction forms part of the open-ended programme covering Prosus shares and Naspers shares and announced in June 2022.

Prosus said the shares were bought at an average price of 36.6009 euros each. The total consideration was 101,755,515.37 euros, equivalent to 114,002,290.17 US dollars. The company did not announce a change to the programme's overall framework in the update.

The latest tranche gives investors a fresh measure of the pace at which Prosus is deploying capital to reduce its share count. Buybacks can support per-share metrics over time, but their effect on the investment case also depends on the performance and valuation of the group's operating portfolio.

Prosus combines interests in food delivery, payments, classifieds, travel, events and other technology businesses with venture investments. That structure leaves the shares exposed both to operating execution and to the market's assessment of the value of listed and private holdings.

Prosus stock traded at 36.98 euros on Lang & Schwarz at 11:14 a.m. CET on Wednesday, November 11. The quoted price stood during the European session, while the buyback announcement referred to purchases completed several days earlier.

Prosus stock faces tougher test as buyback pace slows
sum: Bank of America has added a sharper operating test to the investment case for Prosus. In an analysis published by Finimize on Thursday, November 5, the bank said repurchases have helped contain the holding company's discount to its listed assets, while a slower pace puts more emphasis on portfolio performance.

The latest analysis adds scale to the capital-return story. Bank of America estimates that Prosus has bought back about 30.4 percent of its outstanding shares since June 2022, while parent Naspers has repurchased about 27.8 percent of its own shares. Combined buybacks have reached 49.6 billion US dollars, according to the analysis.

The support is not static. Prosus repurchased about 90 million US dollars of shares in the week from October 26 to October 30, below the roughly 157 million US dollars weekly average since the programme began. If the pace weakens further, the discount will depend more heavily on whether the underlying portfolio delivers stronger growth and profitability.

Bank of America points to Just Eat Takeaway.com and iFood as the key operating areas. Progress at the food-delivery businesses could give investors a second route to a narrower discount, alongside continued share repurchases. The next first-half fiscal update therefore matters not only for earnings, but also for the credibility of Prosus's capital-allocation strategy.

Why the second half of 2026 demands a different investment playbook
sum: If the first half of 2026 has taught investors one lesson, it’s this: markets rarely stick to the script.

At the start of the year, investors expected falling inflation, lower interest rates, and continued dominance by large US technology companies to shape investment returns. Six months later, the picture looks very different.

Inflation has proved more persistent than forecast, prompting central banks to rethink the pace of monetary easing. Oil prices have swung sharply in response to renewed conflict in the Middle East, while market leadership has broadened beyond the large US technology companies that dominated returns over the past two years. Emerging markets have outperformed many developed markets, investors have become far more selective about which AI-driven companies they back, and South Africa has entered the second half of the year with improving economic fundamentals despite a softer equity market.

During its mid-year investment webinar on 23 July, Morningstar Investment Management examined how those shifts have changed the investment outlook – and what they could mean for the portfolios, fund managers, and investment strategies advisers recommend to clients during the remainder of 2026.

At the end of 2025, the consensus was that inflation had largely been brought under control. Central banks had begun cutting interest rates and investors expected that trend to continue through 2026. Instead, inflation has re-emerged as one of the year’s defining risks.

Morningstar attributes much of that shift to energy markets. Renewed conflict in the Middle East pushed Brent crude from about $80 a barrel to above $120 before prices retreated as supply concerns eased. Although oil later recovered, the volatility filtered through to transport costs and consumer prices across many economies.

South Africa has followed a similar pattern. Annual consumer inflation accelerated to 5% in June, its highest level in two years, driven largely by higher fuel and transport costs. Food inflation, by contrast, continued to ease on the back of lower cereal and meat prices and favourable harvests.

South African equities: A cautiously optimistic outlook amidst global uncertainties
sum: Consensus expectations for domestic earnings remain relatively subdued despite a more supportive macro backdrop, improving business confidence, and the prospect of gradually strengthening economic activity over the next year, said Anchor Capital chief investment officers Nolan Wapenaar and Peter Armitage.

In a note on the asset and wealth management, and investment advisory firm’s third quarter strategies, they said geopolitical uncertainty remains elevated, but the broader macroeconomic backdrop has become more constructive, supported by lower energy prices, resilient global growth, improving domestic fiscal fundamentals, and supportive commodity prices, which all provide a favourable environment for risk assets over the medium term.

“Our conviction in SA equities strengthened during the second quarter of 2026, prompting us to move overweight local equities in our strategic asset allocation. We forecast a total return of about 14% over the next 12 months, supported by improving domestic fundamentals, attractive valuations, and potential for a less restrictive US interest-rate environment than is currently reflected in market pricing,” they said.

While both the FTSE/JSE Capped All Share Index and the MSCI South Africa Index declined by 2.4% in the second quarter of 2026, significantly underperforming the MSCI Emerging Markets (+24%) and the MSCI World (+14%) indices, the headline index returns obscured a more encouraging underlying picture, they said.

“The weakness was concentrated in a relatively small number of globally exposed companies rather than reflecting a deterioration in SA’s domestic investment outlook. By contrast, SA government bonds (and the Rand) remained resilient, and a bellwether for domestic equities, the FTSE/JSE Banks Index, advanced by 9.8%, reflecting continued confidence in the local macroeconomic backdrop,” said Wapenaar and Armitage.
Much of the weakness in the local equity market was driven by global rather than local factors and was concentrated in a handful of large index constituents.
Gold and platinum (PGM) producers came under pressure as higher US real yields weighed on precious metal prices.

items.t: Prosus gives irrevocable undertaking to sell residual stake in delivery hero to uber
sum: Prosus N.V. (“Prosus”) announces that it has provided an irrevocable undertaking to Uber Technologies, Inc. (“Uber”) to sell all of its remaining 16.8% stake in Delivery Hero SE (“Delivery Hero”) to Uber upon completion of Uber’s recently announced offer to acquire the share capital in Delivery Hero at a purchase price of €41.50 per ordinary share (the “Offer”). Uber is headquartered in San Francisco, California, United States, and its issued shares are admitted to listing and trading on the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE: UBER), with secondary listings in several stock exchanges across Europe and the Americas.

Under the terms of the European Commission’s approval of the acquisition by Prosus of Just Eat Takeaway.com, Prosus committed to significantly reduce its 26.5% shareholding in Delivery Hero. In compliance with those commitments, on 17 April 2026 Prosus announced the disposal of 13,582,342 ordinary shares it held in Delivery Hero SE to Uber, representing approximately 4.5% of Delivery Hero's issued share capital; and on 11 May 2026, Prosus announced a further disposal of 15,188,284 ordinary shares in Delivery Hero to Aspex Management representing approximately 5% of Delivery Hero's issued share capital.

Prosus now holds a minority stake of 16.8% in Delivery Hero, and Uber holds a stake of 24.99% with a further 11.8% held via instruments. Uber’s Offer represents a significant premium of 151% to Delivery Hero’s 1-month VWAP before the announcement of Prosus’s initial 4.5% stake sale to Uber. Prosus believes that Uber’s offer represents a fair price and effective way to comply with its commitments to the European Commission. Therefore, to support the offer, Prosus has entered into an irrevocable undertaking to Uber to dispose of its remaining interest in Delivery Hero. Prosus intends to use the proceeds of the disposal for general corporate purposes.

The Offer will be subject to, amongst other things, customary regulatory conditions and the Offer then becoming unconditional and proceeding to implementation in accordance with its terms. As such there is no certainty that the Offer will be implemented. The details of the Offer, including the outstanding conditions, are available on Uber’s website: www.uber.com.

Prosus stock advances as share buyback update and Uber Delivery Hero deal reshape portfolio
sum: Prosus stock (ISIN NL0013654783) is in focus on September 7, 2026 after a recent update on its ongoing share repurchase program and confirmation that it plans to sell its roughly 17 percent stake in Delivery Hero into Uber's proposed 15 billion USD takeover, a move that could unlock significant cash for shareholders according to a report by The Daily Star on September 7, 2026. As of the last available close in early September 2026, market data from European trading platforms show Prosus valued at tens of billions of USD, underlining how capital returns and portfolio rotations now drive the investment case. For investors, the combination of buybacks and stake sales is a central theme in assessing Prosus stock.

An official disclosure in the Dutch financial regulator's register dated September 1, 2026 shows Prosus N.V. publishing an 'Update on share repurchase programme', confirming that the company continues to retire shares as part of a broader capital return plan in the AFM register of inside information. In previous phases of its buyback efforts, Prosus has often committed billions of USD to repurchases over multi quarter periods, reducing the free float and consolidating value for remaining shareholders; the latest update indicates that this process is continuing into the second half of 2026. For retail investors, a persistent buyback can mean that even modest earnings growth per share accelerates because the share count shrinks over time.

From a capital allocation perspective, Prosus has historically balanced share repurchases with targeted investments and disposals across its portfolio of internet assets. The current phase of the buyback, as evidenced by the September 2026 AFM filing, suggests that management still sees Prosus stock as undervalued relative to the underlying stakes it holds, especially in large positions such as Tencent. That interpretation matters because when a company buys back stock at a discount to net asset value, each remaining share represents a larger slice of the portfolio than before, effectively increasing per share exposure.

items.t: Naspers' (JSE:NPN) Anemic Earnings Might Be Worse Than You Think
sum: Naspers Limited's (JSE:NPN) recent weak earnings report didn't cause a big stock movement. We think that investors are worried about some weaknesses underlying the earnings.

Importantly, our data indicates that Naspers' profit received a boost of US$4.9b in unusual items, over the last year. While we like to see profit increases, we tend to be a little more cautious when unusual items have made a big contribution. When we crunched the numbers on thousands of publicly listed companies, we found that a boost from unusual items in a given year is often not repeated the next year. Which is hardly surprising, given the name. Naspers had a rather significant contribution from unusual items relative to its profit to March 2026. As a result, we can surmise that the unusual items are making its statutory profit significantly stronger than it would otherwise be.

That might leave you wondering what analysts are forecasting in terms of future profitability. Luckily, you can click here to see an interactive graph depicting future profitability, based on their estimates.

As previously mentioned, Naspers' large boost from unusual items won't be there indefinitely, so its statutory earnings are probably a poor guide to its underlying profitability. For this reason, we think that Naspers' statutory profits may be a bad guide to its underlying earnings power, and might give investors an overly positive impression of the company. But at least holders can take some solace from the 64% per annum growth in EPS for the last three. The goal of this article has been to assess how well we can rely on the statutory earnings to reflect the company's potential, but there is plenty more to consider. If you'd like to know more about Naspers as a business, it's important to be aware of any risks it's facing. At Simply Wall St, we found 2 warning signs for Naspers and we think they deserve your attention.

This note has only looked at a single factor that sheds light on the nature of Naspers' profit. But there are plenty of other ways to inform your opinion of a company. For example, many people consider a high return on equity as an indication of favorable business economics, while others like to 'follow the money' and search out stocks that insiders are buying.

items.t: Naspers hikes dividend by 40% as the Takealot Group hits $1bn in revenue
sum: - Naspers and Prosus reported a 40% climb in their ordinary dividend on Monday, as well as a surge in free cash flow.
- It says its push towards creating consumer internet “ecosystems” with cross-selling opportunities is paying off, including with a 40% jump in revenue at Brazil’s iFood.
- Takealot Group in SA also saw revenue grow by almost a fifth, while it is also looking to scale up its logistics offering.

Naspers, the owner of consumer internet subsidiary Prosus, has reported a climb in its preferred profit measures of more than a tenth on Monday. This includes for local business Takealot Group, which hit $1 billion (R16.4 billion) in revenue for the first time.

Naspers reported that core headline earnings, which exclude non-operational items, rose 14% to $3.6 billion in its year to end March, or by 24% at a per share level. Headline earnings grew just 3.2% to about $2.7 billion, amid a $1.3 billion lower gain on the value of the sale of Tencent shares.

Prosus, the Amsterdam-listed subsidiary of Naspers, held 22.66% of Tencent at period end, and it continues to dominate the group’s about $150 billion in assets. Under CEO Fabricio Bloisi, the group has been making a push to leverage agentic AI and create consumer “ecosystems”, currently focused on Europe, India and Latin America.

Prosus owns large consumer-facing businesses, including iFood in Brazil, fintech PayU in India, the classifieds business OLX, and Despegar, Latin America’s biggest online travel agency. It has made a big push into AI, with its large commerce models, or agentic AI, trained on billions of data points, enabling recommendations and personalisation.

Tencent’s revenue miss heightens pressure for AI payoff
sum: Tencent reported its slowest revenue growth in six quarters, underscoring the urgency around its costly AI pivot while core businesses like games and advertising show signs of age.

Sales for the three months ended March climbed 9% to 196.5 billion yuan (about R476 billion) after the WeChat operator garnered weaker domestic game sales, while net income rose to 58.1 billion yuan, in line with estimates. The underwhelming top-line figure was partially due to the later timing of this year’s Lunar New Year holiday, a traditional catalyst for online entertainment spending.

The lukewarm performance could exacerbate investor concerns about how exactly China’s most valuable company will monetise AI. While Tencent has vowed to at least double investments in the field to more than 36 billion yuan this year, it trails peers like TikTok owner ByteDance and Alibaba Group in terms of both user adoption and advances in developing state-of-the-art large language models.

“Our core businesses continued to grow their engagement, revenue and profit, providing the cash flow to fund our AI investments, as well as use cases for future AI deployment,” Tencent said in its earnings release on Wednesday.

Mirroring their peers in Silicon Valley, Chinese big tech firms are confronting scepticism over the timeline for an AI payoff as ballooning infrastructure costs compress margins. Tencent’s outlay remains among the most conservative of the bunch: Alibaba has pledged a rolling target of more than $50 billion over three years. Taken together, Chinese corporate spending falls drastically short of the hyperscale budgets seen in the US — where the quartet of Amazon, Alphabet, Meta Platforms and Microsoft plans to deploy more than $700 billion this year.

Tencent has shed roughly $160 billion — or 23% — of its market value this year, far exceeding the slide by Alibaba, which reports earnings on the same day. Investors in both Chinese internet icons have recently shifted their focus toward pure-play AI model creators like Zhipu and MiniMax Group, whose valuations have multiplied since their stellar market debuts in January.

Naspers and Prosus shares drop as CEO warns of reduced iFood earnings in 2027
sum: Naspers and its Europe-based internet business Prosus’ share prices fell sharply on the JSE on Tuesday morning after CEO Fabricio Bloisi warned that adjusted earnings for iFood in Brazil would reduce in 2027 because of additional investment required to take on competitors.
Naspers shares traded 5.69% lower on the JSE on Tuesday morning at R839.93, while Prosus shares fell 5.49% to R748.42.

Writing in a letter to shareholders, Bloisi, citing increased competition in the Brazil market, said, “Late in FY26, we stepped up investment (in iFood) and began regrowing market share. We will now accelerate our investment in iFood to take the offensive to stimulate demand and build out and expand successful products…”
This investment would reduce 2027 adjusted earnings before interest, tax, depreciation, and amortisation (EBITDA) to between $100-150 million, he said.

He said, however, that iFood was performing “exceptionally well” and had delivered its 2026 targets. In just a year, its advertising platform had evolved into a meaningful EBITDA contributor, and iFood Pago, a digital bank for restaurants, had reached scale with near triple-digit revenue growth and profitability.

iFood’s meal vouchers business now served over 1 million users and was growing over 100% year-on-year; the in-store business was boosting restaurant partners' earnings, and iFood was also growing strongly in new categories, including pets, beverages, and pharmaceuticals.

The increased investment in iFood was among the group’s priorities for the new 2027 financial year, with other plans including a return to growth at Just Eat Takeaway (JET) in Europe by year-end and more share buybacks.

Prosus sells 5% interest in Delivery Hero for €335m
sum: Prosus has sold a 5% interest in Delivery Hero to Aspex Management for €335m (about R6.5bn) as part of its commitment to European regulatory authorities to significantly reduce its shareholding in the German online takeout business.

In August last year, the European Commission approved Prosus’ acquisition of Just Eat Takeaway.com (Jet), subject to commitments by the Amsterdam-based company to significantly reduce its shareholding in Delivery Hero.
Earlier this year Prosus sold a 4.5% stake in Delivery Hero to Uber for about €270m. It sold about 13.58-million shares in Delivery Hero at €20 per share.

The latest sale to Aspex of about 15.19-million shares has been agreed at €22 per share, representing a 10% premium to the closing share price and a 22% premium to the 30-day volume-weighted average price of Delivery Hero shares as of May 8.
Today’s transaction represents a further step towards fulfilling the commitments to the European Commission, Prosus said.

The transactions come at a time when the European Commission is reported by the Financial Times to be mulling a major overhaul of its rules around merger and competition laws to foster “European champions” capable of competing with US and Chinese rivals.
Amid criticism that strict competition rules and overregulation have stifled innovation on the continent, this move signals a change in tack by the EU.

Prosus stock steady as Brazil antitrust complaint highlights food delivery exposure
sum: Prosus N.V. (ISIN NL0013654783) stock is quoted at 37.05 euros as of September 3, 2026, according to market data that list the share under the PRX.AS ticker on Euronext Amsterdam. The quotation shows a 0.00% daily move at this level, signaling a calm trading day for the tech investment group.

Prosus’ growing footprint in online food delivery is back in the spotlight after Brazil’s antitrust authority Cade ordered a deeper review of competition in the sector following a recent setback for rival Keeta. According to a Reuters report dated September 2, 2026, iFood, a food delivery platform controlled by Prosus, filed a complaint with Cade accusing competitor Keeta of predatory pricing in the Brazilian market.

The same report notes that Cade’s tribunal rejected an appeal by Keeta against exclusivity clauses held by rival platform 99, but simultaneously ordered further investigation into the food delivery sector. For Prosus shareholders, the regulatory review matters because Brazil is one of iFood’s key markets and competition rules can influence commission rates, restaurant access and long term profitability.

Beyond food delivery, Prosus is also using fresh capital to back fast growing digital health and insurance platforms. Business Insider Africa reports that Prosus-backed insurer Alan has entered West Africa by acquiring Tanel Health, gaining about 70,000 members in Senegal and Cote d’Ivoire. According to this article dated September 2, 2026, Prosus invested 400 million euros, approximately 460 million dollars, in Alan through a mix of new and existing shares.

The same source notes that Alan reported annual recurring revenue of more than 800 million euros in the first quarter of 2026, while the Financial Times cited a more recent figure nearer 840 million euros. This combination shows double digit growth in recurring revenue within a short time frame and underlines Prosus’ strategy of backing scalable digital platforms in insurance and health services alongside its better known exposure to internet and e-commerce businesses.
Prosus was carved out as a separate holding company and relisted on Euronext Amsterdam to house Naspers’ international internet assets, including its sizeable stake in Tencent Holdings.

Prosus and Amazon reach AI deal for double-digit cost savings
sum: Prosus, sister company of Naspers, reached a multi-year cloud and artificial-intelligence (AI) deal with an Amazon.com unit that will consolidate contracts in these spheres, resulting in double-digit cost savings.

The three-year pact with Amazon Web Services runs into “hundreds of millions of dollars”, head of Prosus Ecosystem Igor Cardoso said in an interview, declining to disclose the exact value of the deal.

Under CEO Fabricio Bloisi, the group is reorganising itself to focus on Europe, India and Latin America, developing AI capabilities to fast-track and scale its businesses in the three regions to double its value by 2028.

“The strategy is to roll out our large commerce model across Latin America,” where it has Brazilian food delivery and logistics operator iFood, travel business Despegar, and online classifieds firm OLX, said Cardoso. “Then we plan to also do this in Europe and then in India in time.”
While the businesses aren’t able to share data across regions, standardising the models makes it easier and faster to build them in new jurisdictions, said Cardoso.

Prosus has a team of about 1 000 AI specialists who will work with their counterparts at Amazon to co-create applications, Cardoso said, adding that the group is investing about $100 million annually in AI talent and infrastructure.
“In the past 18 to 24 months, we’ve built and deployed agents across our businesses,” Cardoso said. “We are now building and investing in life assistants to support these businesses.”

Coursera to buy Udemy, in which Prosus is an investor
sum: Online education platform Coursera will acquire rival Udemy in an all-stock deal, valuing the combined company at US$2.5-billion, as the industry consolidates after a post-pandemic slowdown and heightened investor scrutiny.

Udemy shareholders will receive 0.8 shares of Coursera for each held, valuing the company at about $930-million. Coursera shares were up about 4%, while Udemy jumped nearly 22%. Prosus, the Amsterdam-headquartered subsidiary of South Africa’s Naspers, holds 12% of Udemy’s shares, according to it website.

Coursera and Udemy bet that a combined platform will be better positioned to capture corporate demand for workforce training, particularly in artificial intelligence, data science and software development, as employers invest in reskilling workers amid rapid advances in generative AI.

“At a high level it seems like this deal makes sense both strategically and financially. We have long viewed a combination of these two companies as compelling given their complementary content offerings and solutions, and the potential for significant cost synergies given overlapping end markets,” said Stephen Sheldon analyst at William Blair.

Based on Coursera’s last close, the offer implies a price of $6.35 per Udemy share, a premium of roughly 18.3%. The companies said the deal is expected to close in the second-half of next year, subject to regulatory and shareholder approvals.

Coursera, which partners with universities and institutions to offer degree programmes and professional certificates, has increasingly focused on enterprise customers, while Udemy operates a marketplace of independent instructors selling individual courses and subscriptions to businesses.

Despite companies pitching AI upskilling as a major growth opportunity, investors have remained cautious on the sector. Shares of online education companies have lagged broader markets amid concerns over competition, pricing pressure and uncertain returns from AI-related investments.
